content_items.title: The BMD Cubing Engine: Harmonizing Biodiversity and Earth Observation Data

programme.title: The BMD Cubing Engine: Harmonizing Biodiversity and Earth Observation Data
programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
programme.abstract:
The Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD) project seeks to provide Natura 2000 site managers with data-driven tools for evidence-based environmental decision-making. Such tools depend on biotic and abiotic datasets to be rendered interoperable in a reproducible manner. Yet the transition from prototype biodiversity data products to operational workflows is hindered by fragmented data sources, inconsistent metadata practices and insufficient preservation of provenance.

To address these challenges, the BMD data cubing engine designs pipelines for producing spatially and temporally harmonized datasets, integrating biodiversity records with Earth Observation (EO) data. The engine generates analysis-ready products that can be reused in downstream modelling and decision-support workflows. A central design principle is provenance preservation: transformations, source datasets and harmonization steps are explicitly captured to support transparency and reproducibility.

This presentation will focus on the practical data model and metadata challenges encountered when aligning EO data with biodiversity observations. Particular attention will be given to metadata interoperability across heterogeneous inputs, in particular the representation of spatial, temporal, taxonomic and methodological context. By presenting the current BMD cubing architecture, we offer a practical contribution to the operational expansion of biodiversity Digital Twin approaches. The proposed design illustrates how FAIR workflows, standardized metadata, and traceable data transformations can support reusable ecological data products for integration into emerging European and global biodiversity data infrastructures.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the convener as 'Matthias Dillen'; he introduces himself as from Meise Botanic Garden and credits colleague Niels (ASR 'Niels Bilit'/'Nils'), who did much of the development but was not present. About two minutes near the start (00:28:51-00:31:22) were lost to getting the slides into presentation mode.

content_items.summary: Mathias Dillen presented the cubing engine built in the Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD) project as the central harmonisation layer between BMD's data catalogue and analytical tools for Natura 2000 site managers. He described a modular Python back end (base grid class, raster/vector engines, a data cube orchestrator with one child class per data source) and a slim front end that takes a YAML 'recipe' and returns harmonised raster and vector files on a common master grid, plus a STAC description and a provenance record. He covered supported sources (GBIF, CHELSA climate data, Earth observation data), GBIF-specific options including Monte Carlo resampling of occurrence uncertainty, and plans to add sources, publish a package and deploy the engine as an API service within BMD.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: BMD's cubing engine turns a declarative YAML recipe into reproducible, provenance-documented data cubes that harmonise GBIF occurrences with climate and Earth observation data on one grid.
content_items.why_it_matters: Harmonising heterogeneous biotic and abiotic data reproducibly is a precondition for decision-support tools; a recipe-driven, extensible engine with STAC and provenance output makes these cubes discoverable and reusable rather than one-off analyses.
key_points: The cubing engine is BMD's central harmonisation layer, feeding harmonised data via an API to analytical tools aimed mainly at Natura 2000 site managers.
It builds on the B3 project's GBIF SQL API 'cube' functionality, which resamples occurrence data and makes heterogeneous data safer to use.

Back end: a base grid class (currently EEA grid, a global equal-area grid and WGS84), raster and vector engines for pure geospatial transformations, and a data cube orchestrator with abstract raster/vector cube classes; each data source is a child class, so adding a source means writing one class.
Front end: a single BMDCube class reads a YAML recipe (global, spatial/temporal and source-specific configuration) and runs the harmonisation without users needing to code.

Output: a data tree of harmonised raster and vector files on the same master grid, a STAC file describing the cube, and a provenance record (runtime, engine and dependency versions, hardware); files can be streamed rather than downloading the whole cube.
Stack: Python with GDAL, GeoPandas, xarray (central data model), Dask/DuckDB; outputs GeoParquet for vectors and NetCDF or Zarr for rasters.
Current sources are GBIF, CHELSA climate data and Earth observation data (being moved to direct access to Copernicus S3 storage).

GBIF options include taxon keys and aggregation ranks, default/min/max coordinate uncertainty, excluding GBIF issue flags, and Monte Carlo resampling of points with fractional grid-cell output or point clouds.
themes_raw: harmonising occurrence and Earth observation data
methods: spatial and temporal harmonisation to a master grid
Monte Carlo resampling of occurrence uncertainty

notable_claims.claim: The engine is designed so that supporting a new data source only requires a new child class implementing access and conversion to the central data model.
Each run produces a provenance record detailing runtime, engine version, dependency versions and the underlying hardware.
Beyond GBIF's own cube functions, the engine supports Monte Carlo resampling of occurrence points, with fractional grid-cell output or point clouds, to account for heterogeneous underlying data.

future_work: Add more data sources under BMD.
Publish the engine as a package, probably after the Earth observation access refactor.
Deploy it as an internal BMD service accessed by analytical tools through an API that manages waiting times and points to streamable outputs.

q_and_a.question: Tanya Berger-Wolf asked how flexible the design is for other ways of organising data, such as repeated surveys and sources like bioacoustics, camera traps and citizen science.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Some support exists (point clouds with uncertainty) and more complex vector objects could be accommodated since GBIF data are mostly points with uncertainty; if the internal data model had to change, new methods and possibly refactoring would be needed.

representative_excerpt.text: And in principle, if you feed that YAML file into this function, and you wait long enough, depending on how heavy the operation is, you get the output without minimal skills in terms of coding notebooks and having to process the code on your end.

notable_moments.description: Architecture of the cubing engine: modular back end and slim front end.
Walk-through of the YAML recipe file and source-specific parameters.
Question on extending the engine to other survey designs and sensor data.

content_items.title: BMD workflow engine: FAIR workflows, RO-Crate and FAIR Signposting for a European biodiversity data space

programme.title: Building the Foundations for a European Biodiversity Data Space
programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
programme.abstract:
European Green Deal Data Spaces serve as catalysts for unlocking data-driven innovation by integrating open and private datasets to help Europe achieve climate neutrality by 2050. By fostering cross-domain collaboration in earth and environmental sciences, economics, and urban planning, these initiatives connect scattered systems into a single, interoperable ecosystem. In the domain of conservation, this is vital for supporting the EU's nature restoration targets and deforestation reduction efforts. Within this strategic context, the Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD) project is actively developing the foundations of a European Biodiversity Data Space.

To enable near-data processing, we are building on workflow.earth, a FAIR-compliant workflow engine engineered originally within the Destination Earth (DestinE) initiative, which is now actively applied to streamline the ecological monitoring of Natura 2000 sites. Leveraging Argo Workflows and declarative pipeline definitions, these workflows fully encapsulate the instructions required for portable, reproducible, and deterministic execution across any Argo-compatible Kubernetes cluster (current in operation at UFZ/JSC and LifeWatch ERIC), while offering researchers a clear, transparent, and readily visualizable view of the underlying scientific processes.

Data portability and workflow transparency are achieved by adopting the Workflow Run RO-Crate (WRROC) specifications. This enables the packaging of workflow definitions, runtime parameters, data outputs, and rich metadata into self-contained FAIR Digital Objects (FDOs). All encapsulated primary data are also preserved as linked data, facilitating the seamless discovery, mobilization, and replication across the broader Common European Data Spaces.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video; the speaker introduces herself as 'Lena Pertzelmaier' (ASR) from Senckenberg, Frankfurt. Co-author Claus Weiland (programme) did not present. The talk focuses on BMD's workflow engine rather than on the data space in general, as the title suggests.

content_items.summary: Lena Perzlmaier presented the workflow engine developed in Biodiversity Meets Data, motivated by letting a Natura 2000 site manager reuse a scientist's species distribution model. She argued that scientists should share code, containerise it, and define a workflow (BMD mainly uses Argo), described with Workflow RO-Crate (prospective provenance) and Workflow Run RO-Crate (retrospective provenance). A central RO-Crate service links user interfaces, execution engines (Workflow.earth on Destination Earth, and the BMD platform's engine at LifeWatch ERIC) and registries, and runs are exposed as FAIR Digital Objects by combining identifiers, RO-Crates and FAIR Signposting.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Packaging containerised workflows and their runs as RO-Crates with FAIR Signposting lets non-technical users run models remotely and get machine-actionable, citable results.
content_items.why_it_matters: It shows a concrete path from 'share your code' to reusable, remotely executable and provenance-rich workflows, which is the practical substance behind data space rhetoric.
key_points: Motivating example: an ecologist's species distribution model reused by a Natura 2000 site manager interested in invasive species spread.
Steps asked of scientists: share code, containerise it, and define a workflow of inputs, steps and outputs; BMD mainly uses Argo and has considered CWL.
Workflow runners can execute on remote infrastructure, so site managers need not run models on limited local hardware.

Workflow RO-Crate adds licence, authorship, description, language and formal inputs/outputs (prospective provenance); Workflow Run RO-Crate adds a CreateAction with agent, actual parameter values and output files (retrospective provenance).

A central RO-Crate service unpacks submitted crates, sends manifests to workflow engines and repackages run results as run crates that can be published to registries (BMD data space, WorkflowHub, Workflow.earth).
Workflow.earth, deployed in Destination Earth, was the first implementation, focused on agricultural digital twins; the BMD platform's engine runs at LifeWatch ERIC.
FAIR Signposting exposes metadata to machines in HTTP headers; combined with a unique identifier and RO-Crate, runs become W3C-style FAIR Digital Objects.
The BMD interface lets users pick a workflow, choose species from a list and an area on a map, and view results in a dashboard or download the run RO-Crate.

notable_claims.claim: Without metadata, a workflow lacks licence, authorship and language information, so users cannot tell whether they may reuse it or whether their engine can run it.
Combining a unique identifier, RO-Crate packaging and FAIR Signposting allows workflow runs to be exposed as FAIR Digital Objects that are both human-readable and machine-actionable.

recommendations: Scientists should publish code, containerise it and define it as a workflow with standard metadata.

representative_excerpt.text: So this way of looking at a workflow is also called the prospective provenance. It is a way of looking at the workflow before it is initiated or before it is executed. It's a kind of a general workflow description, like a recipe that has not yet been executed.

notable_moments.description: Scientist and Natura 2000 site manager example motivating workflow reuse.
Architecture of the RO-Crate service linking interfaces, engines and registries.
BMD user interface: choosing species and area, submitting, viewing a results dashboard.

programme_match.notes: Matched to the programme item; presented by Lena Perzlmaier alone via video. Content centres on the BMD workflow engine within the data space context.

content_items.title: Beyond Data Integration: Ecological and Semantic Interoperability in Coastal Digital Twins

programme.title: Beyond Data Integration: Ecological and Semantic Interoperability in Coastal Digital Twins
programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
programme.abstract:
Coastal zones are highly complex environments that are increasingly affected by sea-level rise, erosion, extreme weather events, biodiversity loss, pollution, and intensifying human activity. The development of coastal zone digital twins brings together diverse data types stemming from multiple domains, including marine science, urban planning, ecology, shipping, fisheries, climate science, and disaster management. The perspectives of these different disciplines and their respective data governance regimes collide, resulting in data integration challenges.

The paper presents a map of coastal zone semantic interoperability challenges, situated in relation to international frameworks including the EIF - European Interoperability Framework. Examples are drawn from a demonstrator twin for Oslofjord, where data is combined from diverse cross-disciplinary observation systems and governance domains. We have organized our map into different classes of problem-types, along with suggestions for tooling and potential solutions. We provide a concrete, practical overview of issues encountered by twin developers, spanning from problematic definitions and ontology misalignment, to inconsistent classifications, divergent coordinate reference systems, fundamental differences in spatial representation, separate metadata standards, temporal mismatches, as well as the limitations of available ontologies. We further cover the non-technical challenges, such as those related to uneven adoption of standards.

The work lays the foundation towards our main goal, “How do we enable a new generation of environmental digital twins that seamlessly integrate biodiversity data between marine, coastal, and terrestrial ecosystems of twins?”

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Laura Slater' (ASR) from SINTEF Digital; she introduces herself as Laura Slaughter. Preceded by about two minutes of slide format problems (PDF vs PowerPoint).

content_items.summary: Laura Slaughter presented a landscape analysis of how far existing standards, data models and interoperability approaches support integrating land and sea data for coastal digital twins, and where the gaps remain. She distinguished digital models, digital shadows (what most demonstrators actually are) and full bidirectional digital twins, noting that SINTEF aims for 'learning twins' that can amend model structure. She then ran through categories of land-sea problems: spatial reference and boundaries (horizontal CRS and vertical datum mismatches, shoreline and boundary definitions), scale and resolution, semantic interoperability, units, technical interoperability, missing data (the 'white ribbon'), provenance and governance.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Coastal digital twins expose a long list of unresolved land-sea interoperability gaps, from vertical datums and shifting shorelines to missing cross-domain ontologies.
content_items.why_it_matters: Anyone building digital twins that span terrestrial and marine domains will hit these problems; a structured map of existing support and gaps helps decide where to invest.
key_points: Norway's long coastline has produced several coastal twin projects (coastal change, storm simulators), where marine and terrestrial data 'clash'.
Work was a landscape analysis: derive digital twin requirements from the literature, then map land-sea integration problems, who works on them and remaining gaps.
Digital model (no automated link), digital shadow (automatically updated from the physical system but not acting back) and digital twin (bidirectional) are distinct; many demonstrators are shadows.
The goal is learning twins that can recommend interventions and amend both state and model structure, which raises requirements such as dynamic data integration and handling missing data.

Spatial issues: horizontal CRS mismatches (partly addressed, e.g. by OGC), vertical datum mismatch between land elevation and marine depth, dynamic shorelines, land-sea boundary semantics and geometry mismatches.
Semantic issues: incomplete cross-domain feature mappings, one concept with different names or definitions, need for cross-domain ontologies; units remain a problem.
Technical issues include schema, format and API incompatibilities; static integration becomes outdated, so dynamic integration with minimal information loss is needed.
The 'white ribbon' is the coastal zone too deep for terrestrial surveys and too shallow for ships, where data are largely missing.
questions: How should effort be prioritised across the many land-sea interoperability gaps?

notable_claims.claim: Many of the demonstrators SINTEF has built are digital shadows rather than true bidirectional digital twins.
Land elevations and marine depths often use different vertical datums, which remains a problem for coastal twins.
The 'white ribbon' coastal zone, too deep for terrestrial surveys and too shallow for ships, is characterised by missing data.

recommendations: Develop explicit land-sea cross-domain mappings, shared vocabularies and cross-domain ontologies.
Move from static to dynamic data integration with minimal information loss.
results_findings: A landscape map of existing support and gaps for land-sea integration in digital twins, to be made available.
limitations: Preliminary work; the speaker ran out of time and only skimmed several categories.
future_work: Solutions will be pursued across upcoming projects; the speaker is most interested in semantic interoperability, but geospatial issues must also be resolved.

q_and_a.question: Gabi (a session organiser) asked how she sees the solutions coming.
q_and_a.answer_summary: The work is preliminary and meant to decide where to focus; solutions will come in different upcoming projects, with her own interest in semantic interoperability alongside geospatial problems.

representative_excerpt.text: And this is where you have a digital representation is automatically updated by the physical system, but it does not automatically act back on it. So quite a lot of the demonstrators which we've made are actually digital shadows.

notable_moments.description: Research question of the landscape analysis on land-sea integration for digital twins.
Digital model vs digital shadow vs digital twin.
The 'white ribbon' coastal data gap.

content_items.title: From Buzzwords to Blueprints: What It Really Takes to Operationalise Biodiversity Digital Twins

programme.title: From Buzzwords to Blueprints: What It Really Takes to Operationalise Biodiversity Digital Twins
programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
programme.abstract:
The language of Digital Twins and Data Spaces has rapidly entered biodiversity monitoring and conservation but what does operational reality actually require? In this talk, I move past the buzzwords to examine the concrete components that determine how a Digital Twin transitions from prototype to sustained infrastructure, and where this fits into the emerging Data Space ecosystem.

Drawing on experience from BioDT, DTO-BioFlow, and Biodiversity Meets Data (BMD), I identify building blocks that make the difference. Operationalisation demands more than a working pipeline: it requires interoperable metadata patterns, robust provenance preservation, and honest engagement with real-world metadata quality problems. I illustrate this through concrete examples where metadata and crosswalks become decisive. For instance, harmonising Annex I habitat types across EEA Natura 2000 datasets to reconciling marine functional trait vocabularies. These are not edge cases; how we handle them determines whether data can actually flow between systems. We can also learn from the earth observation use cases, where the combination of Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) and SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC), and cloud object storage represents something more fundamental than technical convenience: a set of contracts between producers and consumers governing access patterns, discoverability, and long-term availability. This architecture is what makes scalable services possible, and offers a model for operationalising biodiversity twins and connecting them into a data space.

I conclude by situating these technical foundations within the institutional architectures the session addresses and outline what a shared metadata and interoperability contract could look like.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by the convener as 'Sherif'; affiliation inferred from his later remark that the BMD data cube has to run at Naturalis. Presented fourth, as scheduled.

content_items.summary: Sharif Islam used the Gartner hype cycle to argue that buzzwords like 'digital twin' and 'data space' help win funding but do not help once projects start. His blueprint places the real work in a middle 'control plane' of context, discovery, governance and contracts between fragmented data sources and the consumers (media, funders, policymakers) that buzzwords address. Drawing on BioDT, he said FAIR digital twins boil down to metadata profiles and cross-domain mappings; for BMD he described a STAC-based catalogue with GeoParquet and cloud-native formats so users can query and fetch only the slices they need, including the cubes from the cubing engine.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Use buzzwords to get funded, then break them down into concrete blueprints: metadata, catalogues, governance and stewardship in the middle layer.
content_items.why_it_matters: It gives a pragmatic framing for turning digital twin and data space funding language into implementable components, and names governance and stewardship as work that must be resourced.
key_points: Digital twin peaked on Gartner's 2018 hype cycle; by 2025 it had been replaced by agents and physical AI, while BioDT (2022) and DTO-BioFlow (2023) were funded on the term.
Buzzwords help proposals but when real work starts teams must still define what a digital twin or data space actually is.
The blueprint: fragmented sources on one side, consumers on the other, and a middle layer of context, discovery, governance and contracts that can be centralised or federated.

BioDT experience: FAIR for digital twins boils down to metadata; human communication issues (e.g. 'model calibration' vs 'model training') required mandatory metadata profiles (model version, datasets, inputs/outputs) and mappings.

In BMD, heterogeneous inputs (Natura 2000 boundaries, EEA species checklists, camera trap and eDNA surveys) are brought together via the cubing engine and a centralised metadata catalogue, plus access control for restricted species.
STAC is a simple static-JSON metadata catalogue with a common API and search; with GeoParquet it can index many S3 objects and supports geospatial and metadata queries.
Cloud-native formats let users take only the slice they need instead of downloading huge CSV files; cubes can likewise be sliced for different audiences.
TDWG standards are foundational, alongside OGC and other standards; governance and stewardship of data and models must be part of the blueprint.

notable_claims.claim: In BioDT, making digital twins FAIR came down largely to metadata, requiring mandatory profile elements such as model version, datasets, inputs and outputs.
Without the middle control plane of context, discovery and governance, consumers and services probably will not be able to do anything with fragmented data sources.

recommendations: Use buzzwords to win funding, then break them down into a concrete blueprint.
Invest in the middle layer of discovery, metadata and governance, including stewardship of both data and models.

representative_excerpt.text: So in conclusion, basically, buzzwords are there. We have to use them to get the funding. But after the funding is received, use the buzzword and break it down to a blueprint to get something useful.

notable_moments.description: 'Punchline' blueprint slide: the middle layer of context and discovery.
STAC catalogue approach for BMD.
Buzzwords for funding, blueprints for work.

content_items.title: Digital Twins as System-Optimization Tools: Provisioning Edge and Cloud Infrastructure for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale

programme.title: Digital Twins as System-Optimization Tools: Provisioning Edge and Cloud Infrastructure for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale
programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
programme.abstract:
Monitoring dynamic ecosystems increasingly requires autonomous systems that make decisions at the far edge, where sensors meet the environment. Biodiversity digital twins, however, are typically positioned as integration and visualization layers over data streams produced by sensor networks whose hardware, models, and edge-cloud placement have already been fixed. This framing treats the cyber-physical system as fixed and external. We argue that monitoring biodiversity at landscape scale should be approached as a system-optimization problem, and operational DTs must model and help provision the cyberphysical system itself, including the edge AI stack where most decisions are made.

Autonomous ecosystem sensing must balance processing speed, energy use, network availability, and ecological goals in ways single-platform designs cannot resolve. Smart sensors, powered by edge AI, close a local loop at the edge; coordinating them across modalities, sites, and ecosystems is a provisioning decision with ecological consequences. Where to place a sensor or model, when to offload to the cloud, and how mission settings interact with accuracy are decisions a data-only DT cannot represent, let alone optimize.

Robotics-readiness requires embodied intelligence, where models, sensors, and platforms act on the world they observe. Extending DT architectures to support this requires co-simulating layers that data-only DTs treat as out of scope, combining ecological realism with edge-deployed AI models, smart sensors, and edge-to-cloud networks. We argue that modeling the cyberphysical system, including the dynamic ecosystems it observes, is what makes DTs operational and necessary infrastructure for biodiversity monitoring at scale.

actual.identification_notes: Presented by Tanya Berger-Wolf, who said she was 'impersonating' Jenna Kline (ASR 'Jenna Klein'), her former PhD student now a postdoc at MIT, and the student team who did the work. Affiliation inferred from her description of The Wilds as about an hour from her university.

content_items.summary: Tanya Berger-Wolf argued that biodiversity digital twins should model not only nature but also the sensing system itself, so that deployments of drones, camera traps, acoustic sensors, GPS tags and supporting compute, power and network infrastructure can be planned and optimised. Using a summer deployment at The Wilds conservation centre in Ohio (over 400,000 data points across five modalities), she showed a mock-up in which camera trap positions and drone flight plans can be moved within the twin. She called for bringing robotics and sensor-system standards into the same conversation as data standards and AI readiness, pointing to simulators such as WildWing.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Digital twins should close the sim-to-real loop for the sensor systems too, letting teams plan where and how to deploy multimodal monitoring before going into the field.
content_items.why_it_matters: At-scale monitoring (e.g. the newly announced Amazon.ia effort) depends on deploying complementary sensors in the right place and time; treating the cyber-physical system as part of the twin makes that a solvable optimisation problem.
key_points: Remote sensing, autonomous vehicles, on-body sensors, camera traps, acoustic recorders, eDNA and citizen science capture complementary signals at different spatiotemporal scales.
At-scale monitoring requires cross-modal coordination and provisioning of compute, energy, infrastructure and sensor deployment ('sensing everything, everywhere, all at once').
Current practice stops at data analysis; the loop should return to system refinement, using digital experiments in the twin to plan future deployments.

The Wilds (Ohio), a large conservation science site with endangered species, was instrumented over a summer, yielding over 400,000 data points across GPS tags, camera traps, acoustic sensors, drone flights and citizen science.
A mock-up twin lets users reposition camera traps and edit drone flight plans with full sensor details to see what the system needs to provision.
Standards now exist for biodiversity data and AI readiness is being discussed; robotics and sensor aspects need to join the same conversation.
Simulation environments already exist for drones, e.g. the WildWing software for drone mission planning in biodiversity settings.
A FAIR4AI drone data standard was to be presented virtually by Jenna Kline later the same day.
questions: How far can digital twins be used to decide where to put compute, network relays and power in remote landscapes?

notable_claims.claim: Over a summer deployment at The Wilds, the team collected over 400,000 data points across five modalities: GPS tags, camera traps, acoustic sensors, drone flights and citizen science.
Most integration currently stops at data analysis rather than feeding back into refining the sensing system.

recommendations: Include the hardware, sensor and compute infrastructure in biodiversity digital twins so deployments can be planned in simulation.

q_and_a.question: Sharif Islam asked how drones and instruments from commercial partners fit into an open research ecosystem.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Hardware may be commercial but everything built on top is open: computer vision and coordination models, system planning and provisioning models, and environments like WildWing; Jenna Kline has shown drone systems can be built from off-the-shelf and open source components.

representative_excerpt.text: And so digital twins, we argue that digital twins must capture not just the virtual realism of the nature, but also the system infrastructure built in together.

notable_moments.description: Argument that twins must include the sensing system infrastructure.
Mock-up twin with movable camera trap placements and drone flight plans.
Question about commercial hardware in open research.

content_items.title: How to operationalize large-scale aerial biodiversity monitoring?

programme.title: How to operationalize large-scale aerial biodiversity monitoring?

speakers.name: Peter Desmet
speakers.affiliation: Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO)

programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
programme.abstract:
At the time of this conference, millions of songbirds are migrating south across Europe. Many do this at high altitudes and under the cover of darkness, making it hard to monitor them at scale with citizen science or bio-logging. Weather radars can detect these aerial movements, 24/7, through an existing network that covers most of continental Europe.

Over the last decade, the radar aeroecology community has developed methods to extract biological signals from weather radar data. Through the Aloft data portal (https://aloftdata.eu), these data are now available from 2012 onwards for 181 radars in 24 European countries and updated near real-time. The resulting biological data consists of vertical profiles time series (VPTS) with the speed, direction and density of animals aloft. The data are standardized following the VPTS CSV standard and can be accessed, processed and visualized through a number of open source software tools (getRad, bioRad, CROW).

While these data do not contain species-level information, they are an important quantitative source used to study biomass flows, migration timing and aerial habitat use. They have also enabled the development of migration prediction models, which are important for flight safety, collision prevention, disease spread modelling and public outreach.

To truly evolve to a digital twin of the sky, the Aloft data portal needs to address a number of key challenges. Funding for maintaining software and infrastructure is limited, access to unfiltered weather radar data remains an issue, and methodological work is needed to better separate bird and insect signals. By collaborating with other biodiversity infrastructures, we hope we can continue to provide and expand radar-derived data products for policy and research in Europe.

speakers.name: Peter Desmet
speakers.affiliation: Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO)

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Peter Desmet'/'Pieter'; affiliation from general knowledge (not stated in the recording). ASR renders the vol2bird algorithm as 'Volto Bird'/'default to bird', the radar aeroecology community as 'radar aviary ecology' and the visualisation tool as 'CRO'.

content_items.summary: Peter Desmet explained how European weather radars, which scan the sky continuously for precipitation, also detect nocturnal bird migration, and how the vol2bird algorithm extracts altitude, speed, direction and density of 'meat in the sky' (no species information). The radar aeroecology community has produced the VPTS CSV standard (Frictionless table schema), a maintained radar metadata list, open-source packages and the Aloft data portal, archiving derived vertical profile data for 24 countries and 173 radars back to 2012, updated daily and archived on Zenodo under CC0. He outlined an aerial-habitat digital twin for migration forecasting (collision prevention, avian flu) modelled on the US BirdCast, and noted obstacles: filtered data from meteorological institutes, lack of taxonomy, and a small community maintaining infrastructure.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Existing weather radar networks already monitor bird migration continent-wide; with open standards and the Aloft archive, they could underpin a European migration-forecasting digital twin.
content_items.why_it_matters: It turns an existing sensor network into a biodiversity monitoring infrastructure at no deployment cost and raises the broader question of how to publish probabilistic, non-specimen observations.
key_points: Songbirds migrate mostly at night, at high altitude and on a broad front, making them hard to monitor with citizen science or GPS tags.
Weather radars emit microwaves up to about 35 km from the radar; birds are separated from rain by more variable speed/direction and lower reflectivity.
vol2bird extracts altitude, speed, direction and density, converting reflectivity to numbers of average-size songbirds; species are unknown.

Community standards include the VPTS CSV format for vertical profile time series (defined with Frictionless table schema), a format for raw polar volumes, and a co-maintained list of European radars that tracks code changes.

Meteorological institutes typically keep data only about two days, so the community archives derived biological data in the Aloft portal: 24 countries, 173 radars, back to 2012, nearly 5,000 days, CC0 on Zenodo, updated daily with a 1-2 day delay.
Open-source packages support discovery, visualisation and analysis; a visualisation tool shows near-real-time migration, e.g. a radar south of Oslo and Karlskrona.
An aerial digital twin could support migration forecasting for wind turbine and aircraft collision prevention, disease modelling (avian flu), outreach, and a biomass essential biodiversity variable.
BirdCast in the US, using NOAA's unified radar network, forecasts migration three days ahead (e.g. 340 million birds in one night).

content_items.title: Operationalising biodiversity DT ecosystems through assessment-driven service mapping and reusable tools and workflow integration

programme.title: Operationalising biodiversity DT ecosystems through assessment-driven service mapping and reusable tools and workflow integration
programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems
programme.abstract:
Operationalising biodiversity Digital Twin (DT) ecosystems requires interoperable, reusable, and scalable integration of data, services, and workflows across distributed environmental infrastructures. This work proposes an assessment-driven framework for biodiversity and bioflow DT ecosystems based on service mapping, reusable analytical components, and workflow integration to support operational deployment across biodiversity and marine domains. The approach, tested through HE BioDT and continued in HE BioFLow, systematically identifies, evaluates, and connects datasets, models, computational services, and stakeholder requirements into interoperable workflows adaptable across applications and regions.

The assessment framework reduces fragmentation between platforms and solutions while enhancing transparency, reproducibility, and findability of biodiversity DT implementations. We propose an approach integrating environmental resources through standardised interfaces and modular tools, where assessment-driven matching enables identification of suitable execution and operational environments.

In this context, Data Spaces can benefit from biodiversity DT ecosystems by providing operational environments where FAIR data, services, and analytical workflows can be shared, reused, and connected across domains.

The proposed framework contributes to the objectives of the European Mission “Restore our Ocean and Waters” by supporting assessment of DT ecosystems for improved environmental intelligence and evidence-based decision support for marine and coastal resilience.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Sirine'/'Shirin' (ASR); she introduces herself as from TNO, the Netherlands. The last question (02:08:46) was posed as a transition into the discussion.

content_items.summary: Syrine Ben Aziza argued that biodiversity digital twin projects keep producing tools that are hard to find, understand and adopt once funding ends, so similar solutions get rebuilt. TNO's 'assessment tech' approach pairs 'what is needed' (purpose, stakeholders, capabilities and maturity) with 'what is available' (solutions and resources) through five steps: define context, compare capabilities with needs, identify gaps and constraints, match goals to options, and check feasibility, iteratively. She described a use case guide in BioDT for teams to assess their twin's maturity and ambition, and in DTO-BioFlow an inventory of existing tools tagged by technicalities, infrastructure needs and limitations matched to demonstrator use cases' needs gathered by questionnaire; next steps are automation in the Digital Twin of the Ocean context and eventual standardisation.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A simple, purpose-first assessment that maps a team's needs and capabilities to an inventory of existing tools helps digital twin projects reuse rather than rebuild.
content_items.why_it_matters: Tool reuse and sustainability are chronic problems in project-funded biodiversity infrastructure; a lightweight assessment method targets the non-technical barriers of discovery, expertise and adoption.
key_points: Tools built 'in a bubble' for specific contexts are difficult to find, reuse and adopt; documentation is often not understood by domain scientists without IT support.
Resource and maintenance requirements deter adoption, leading to duplicated solutions and a cycle of prototypes.
The approach asks 'what is needed' (purpose, stakeholders, capabilities, maturity) and 'what is available' (solutions, resources), then maps them to reveal gaps.
Five steps: define current context; compare capabilities with needs; identify gaps and constraints; match goals to options; check feasibility of implementation, with feedback between steps.
In BioDT, a use case guide let teams assess their twin's state and ambition (e.g. whether a dynamic twin is actually needed) before technical decisions.

In DTO-BioFlow, existing tools were summarised with keyword tags (technicalities, infrastructure needs, limitations), and demonstrator needs were gathered by structured questionnaire and mapped into thematic areas.
Next: make the approach more automated and validated in the Digital Twin of the Ocean / Mission Ocean context (ASR 'Oceanity'), and eventually standardise repeatable patterns.
questions: How can requirement elicitation results be kept in machine-readable form for future twins?

notable_claims.claim: Understanding development needs and purpose before diving into technicalities greatly helped BioDT teams make later technical decisions.
Mapping DTO-BioFlow use cases to an inventory of existing tools let use cases find solutions and get support from other technical teams.

recommendations: Start from the purpose and users of a digital twin before choosing technology.
Make room in proposals for sharing existing tools and inventories across partners.
limitations: Requirement elicitation results are kept in project reports but are not machine-readable.
future_work: Automate and validate the assessment approach in the Digital Twin of the Ocean context.
Standardise patterns that repeat across domains while keeping necessary tailoring.
examples_case_studies: DTO-BioFlow tool inventory and demonstrator mapping

q_and_a.question: Sharif Islam asked how to handle mismatched institutional processes when two or three organisations must work together.
q_and_a.answer_summary: That goes beyond the assessment approach; it needs coalitions or agreements from the start, room in proposals for sharing inventories, and demonstrated outcomes to overcome bureaucratic obstacles while protecting intellectual property.

q_and_a.question: Ana asked whether the elicited user requirements are captured as machine-readable information for future reuse.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Learnings are coded into proofs of concept, and information is kept in project reports, but it is not machine-readable.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether the approach translates to tech transfer to industry and conservation organisations.
q_and_a.answer_summary: The approach was inspired by industrial assessments of SME digitalisation maturity, simplified and stripped of industry jargon for biodiversity.

representative_excerpt.text: But if we look globally at what is happening in the biodiversity digital twin landscape and initiatives and all of these great projects, it is often that we do produce a lot of tools, a lot of solutions, but then once the funding is over or the project is over, we forget about these tools, or we move on to other new solutions.

notable_moments.description: 'What is needed' vs 'what is available' framing.
The five-step assessment process.

content_items.title: Post-BioDT lessons and next-generation biodiversity digital twins

programme.title: Discussion
programme.session: SYM15 Operationalizing Biodiversity Digital Twins within Data Space Ecosystems

actual.identification_notes: Moderated by a convener who frames 'post-BioDT lessons' and closes by thanking the organisers (Hannah, Dag, Gabi, Sharif, Niels), so almost certainly Claus Weiland; affiliation Senckenberg per the Lena Perzlmaier talk's reference to 'Klaus' team'. content_items.summary: The convener framed the discussion around the lesson from BioDT that biological and ecological complexity could not be captured by large monolithic twins like Destination Earth's climate twins, leaving many specialised prototypes reliant on GBIF, LifeWatch and DiSSCo, and asked what a next-generation biodiversity digital twin should look like. A BioDT work package lead said twinning nature is naive and the project's lasting outcome was educational: modellers and data communities came to understand each other. Others stressed that users never asked for digital twins and simpler tools may solve problems, that outside Europe work must be decentralised (NEON, LTER, GBIF, iNaturalist, Amazon.ia), that twins risk being 'theatre' offering an illusion of control while habitat is destroyed, and that rapid-response twins for emerging threats could be valuable. It closed with a call to continue at an RDA digital twins session in London.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: BioDT delivered pilots and, above all, mutual understanding between modellers and data people; the next generation must find real users and real conservation impact rather than chase the digital twin label.
content_items.why_it_matters: It is a candid, insider assessment of what a large EU biodiversity digital twin project did and did not achieve, useful for anyone designing follow-on infrastructure or funding calls.
key_points: Large infrastructures like Destination Earth excel at continuous climate/meteorological data, but monolithic twins could not capture ecological modelling complexity.
BioDT produced a gradient of pilot twins from simple to complex; they promised pilots and delivered pilots.
The most lasting BioDT outcome was educational: modellers stopped assuming data 'fall from the sky' and data communities began to understand modellers.
Communication between data scientists, biologists and social scientists improved; BMD's cubing work continues BioDT lessons.
No scientist or user asked for a 'digital twin' or 'data space'; simpler tools that solve the problem may be fine and should be advertised as such.
Outside Europe there is little centralised funding; decentralised or semi-centralised networks (NEON, LTER, GBIF, NatureServe, iNaturalist, STRI, Amazon.ia) are testbeds for transferring methods.
Standards have progressed from FAIR data to open code, AI models and now workflows.
Global Nature Watch lacked occurrence data, suggesting occurrence data could fill a gap in large AI platforms.
Twins risk being theatre giving funders an illusion of control while habitats are destroyed; the 'then what' of real conservation impact is unresolved.
Quickly spun-up twins could help respond to emerging threats such as avian flu, invasive crop pathogens and zoonoses.
Open data can be perceived as a threat (e.g. Finnish forest landowners), making data policy interoperability a concern.
questions: How would a next-generation biodiversity digital twin project look?
How can biodiversity digital twins make a difference on the ground in land-use planning and conservation?
How far can tools from centralised projects be generalised to highly distributed systems?

After BioDT, it is not yet clear how biodiversity digital twins make a difference on the ground.

content_items.title: Toward Quantitative AI-Readiness Metrics for Biodiversity Data Infrastructures

programme.title: Toward Quantitative AI-Readiness Metrics for Biodiversity Data Infrastructures
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: As AI becomes increasingly integrated into biodiversity research, the need for biodiversity data that are not only FAIR but also machine-actionable, interoperable, and reproducible has become increasingly apparent. While biodiversity repositories continue to expand access to specimen, image, and trait data, there remains no widely adopted framework for evaluating how effectively these datasets support AI-driven workflows. Current biodiversity standards primarily emphasize data sharing and interoperability for human use, but often lack mechanisms for assessing suitability for machine reasoning, computer vision, automated metadata generation, or large language model integration. This presentation examines the emerging concept of “AI-readiness” in biodiversity informatics and proposes a framework for developing quantitative AI-readiness metrics for biodiversity data infrastructures. Potential dimensions include metadata completeness, semantic consistency, provenance transparency, image processability, workflow reproducibility, interoperability of derived data products, and machine-actionable linkages among specimens, media, and traits. The talk will explore how AI-readiness evaluation may support automated quality assessment, benchmarking across repositories, and reproducible AI workflows. Using examples from biodiversity imaging and AI-assisted collection workflows, this presentation discusses how quantitative evaluation frameworks may help identify standards gaps and support the development of interoperable and provenance-aware biodiversity infrastructures aligned with emerging AI applications. Particular attention will be given to the role of TDWG standards and community coordination in defining shared metrics and best practices for AI-ready biodiversity ecosystems.

actual.identification_notes: Session convener presenting his own talk directly after a short introduction. ASR renders Fish-AIR as 'Fish-AEAR', TDWG as 'TADWIC/TABIC' and Audiovisual Core as 'Audio-Visual Core'/'Odonton Core'; the task group name is rendered 'AIQAER' and could not be confirmed.

content_items.summary: Yasin Bakış defined AI readiness as the degree to which a dataset and its workflows can support a defined AI task reliably, reproducibly and interoperably, and argued it should be task-specific, multi-dimensional, testable and expressed as a profile rather than a single global score. Drawing on work preparing museum fish images from GBIF, iDigBio and museums for machine learning, he described moving from manual to automated metadata capture and feeding task performance (e.g. from a trait-extraction landmarking pipeline) back into the profile. Finding that about 90-95% of their roughly 200 needed terms were absent from Darwin Core, Audiovisual Core, EXIF and PROV, the team built the Fish-AIR platform and vocabulary and a TDWG task group under Audiovisual Core.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: AI readiness should be a task-specific, measurable profile rather than a single score, and current biodiversity standards lack most of the terms needed to describe it.
content_items.why_it_matters: It makes AI readiness operational and exposes a concrete vocabulary gap in TDWG standards for image-based machine learning, with a route to address it via a task group.
key_points: Definition: the degree to which a dataset and its associated workflows can support a defined AI task reliably, reproducibly and interoperably.
AI readiness is task-specific, multi-dimensional, testable and profile-based; there should be a readiness profile, not a global score.
Profile dimensions include metadata completeness, semantic alignment, provenance, image (data) suitability, reproducibility, interoperability and task performance.
Metadata completeness is not just the share of filled columns but whether the fields ML practitioners use for filtering and cleaning are present.
Manual metadata capture was too slow and expensive, so automated metadata capture was adopted.
An AI-ready dataset is expected to perform better but does not guarantee good results; task performance scores from a trait-extraction/landmarking pipeline update the profile.
Of roughly 200 terms developed, about 90-95% were new, not found in Darwin Core, Audiovisual Core, EXIF, PROV or other standards.

Fish-AIR supplies data and metadata to ML researchers, iterates on their complaints and generates vocabulary passed to the TDWG task group, Audiovisual Core and data quality groups, then to repositories like GBIF, DiSSCo and Phenoscape.
methods: task performance feedback from landmarking pipelines

notable_claims.claim: Of about 200 terms the team needed to describe AI readiness of image datasets, roughly 90-95% were not available in existing standards such as Darwin Core, Audiovisual Core, EXIF or PROV.
An AI-ready dataset is expected to perform better but does not guarantee good results.

recommendations: Express AI readiness as a task-specific profile rather than a single global score.
Share experiences across taxonomic communities and join or brief the TDWG task group.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether Fish-AIR is fish-specific or usable in other domains.
q_and_a.answer_summary: It is currently fish-specific but designed to be extensible to other taxa and AI tasks by adding columns defined in one's own vocabulary; the generalised concept is 'X-AIR' (e.g. 'Butterfly-AIR').

representative_excerpt.text: And my definition is AI readiness is the degree to which a data set and its associated workflows can support a defined AI task reliably, reproducibly, and interoperably.

notable_moments.description: AI readiness as a profile rather than a single score.
Most needed terms were missing from existing standards.

content_items.title: Traits Thesaurus: toward semantic harmonization of FAIR trait-based data on aquatic organisms

programme.title: Traits Thesaurus: toward semantic harmonization of FAIR trait-based data on aquatic organisms
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Trait-based approaches are increasingly important in biodiversity and ecological research, particularly for assessing community and ecosystem responses to biodiversity loss and environmental change. Functional traits provide essential information linking species and community characteristics to ecosystem functioning across spatial and temporal scales. However, the growing use of trait-based methods across ecological domains has highlighted the lack of harmonised trait definitions, terminologies, and measurement units. This semantic heterogeneity limits interoperability, data integration, and reuse of trait information across studies, taxa, and ecosystems, representing a major barrier to large-scale biodiversity synthesis. To address these limitations, we developed the Traits Thesaurus, a controlled vocabulary containing more than 1,500 standardised trait concepts for aquatic organisms. The thesaurus unifies and significantly expands five existing vocabularies dedicated to Phytoplankton, Macroalgae, Zooplankton, Macrozoobenthos, and Fish traits within a single interoperable framework. Its development followed a collaborative, community-endorsed development and validation process involving more than 40 experts from different ecological and biodiversity research domains. The resource provides stable URIs, clear definitions, preferred and alternative labels, and semantic mappings to external vocabularies and ontologies. Designed according to FAIR and Linked Open Data principles, the Traits Thesaurus supports semantic annotation, interoperability, and integration across biodiversity information systems and ecological disciplines, facilitating large-scale data mobilisation and advancing trait-based biodiversity and ecosystem research.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Jessica Titocchi' (ASR). She is also affiliated with LifeWatch ERIC / LifeWatch Italy. ASR renders VocBench as 'Bokbench' and EcoPortal as 'Ecoportal'.

content_items.summary: Jessica Titocci presented the Trait Thesaurus, a SKOS thesaurus developed with LifeWatch Italy to harmonise functional trait terminology for aquatic organisms. She described the heterogeneity of trait data (sources, aggregation levels, repositories, structures) and especially semantic heterogeneity, such as 'body size' meaning prosome length for copepods. Four separate domain thesauri (fish, macroalgae, phytoplankton, zooplankton) were merged by manual and automated ontology alignment into a unified resource of over 1,500 concepts (now five schemes including macrobenthos) published on EcoPortal, with URIs, synonyms, definitions, units and SKOS mappings to existing resources. It is used for semantic annotation in LifeWatch Italy's portal and in projects like PoMP.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A community-validated SKOS thesaurus of aquatic trait terms and units can make open trait data genuinely interoperable across taxa.
content_items.why_it_matters: Open trait data are not automatically reusable; shared definitions are needed for cross-taxa synthesis and for AI/NLP applications on trait data.
key_points: Trait data come from literature, collections, in situ monitoring and remote sensing, at individual, species or community level, quantitative or qualitative, in varied repositories and structures.
Semantic heterogeneity is the hardest problem: different terms for the same thing and the same term with different meanings (e.g. body size vs prosome length in copepods).
Development steps: scoping, term gathering, formalisation (SKOS data model, VocBench editor), then editing and community validation before publication.
Four independent domain thesauri (fish, macroalgae, phytoplankton, zooplankton) were aligned manually and automatically into one Trait Thesaurus of more than 1,500 concepts.
Now five schemes (including macrobenthos); each term has a preferred label, URI, synonyms, definition, scheme membership, units and SKOS closeMatch/exactMatch mappings.
Published on EcoPortal; used for semantic annotation of datasets, metadata and attributes in the LifeWatch Italy data portal and metadata catalogue.
Applied to harmonise plankton datasets in the Polar Ocean Mitigation Potential (PoMP) project and in progress for a coral reef benthic database.
A LifeWatch working group on traits and a SCOR working group for zooplankton are being launched.

notable_claims.claim: The unified Trait Thesaurus contains more than 1,500 concepts.
Making trait data open does not necessarily make them FAIR and reusable, largely because of semantic heterogeneity.

recommendations: Adopt the thesaurus to annotate trait datasets and contribute terms via the new working groups.
future_work: Add multilingual labels, starting with preferred labels and synonyms, then definitions.
Continue community-driven expansion and refinement; possible collaboration with TDWG.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether it is English-only, since their museum has Dutch terms.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Multilingual support is planned, starting with translated preferred labels and synonyms, then definitions.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether she works with a TDWG task group on this, and if not why not.
q_and_a.answer_summary: This was her first TDWG; she was not aware of the opportunity but would welcome it.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether correspondences with concepts in existing ontologies are preserved.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Alignments were found mostly manually and recorded as close or exact matches; existing terms were imported with their original URIs, and new terms were created only where aquatic morphological traits were missing.

representative_excerpt.text: Indeed, when we talk about traits, we often use different terminologies for meaning the same thing, or we use same terminologies, but actually, these same terminologies applied in different contexts can have different meaning.

notable_moments.description: 'Body size' means prosome length for copepods: semantic heterogeneity example.
Merging four domain thesauri into one unified resource.

content_items.title: Provenance, Lineage, and Auditability in AI-Driven Biodiversity Image Workflows

programme.title: Provenance, Lineage, and Auditability in AI-Driven Biodiversity Image Workflows
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: As the role of artificial intelligence in biodiversity research becomes increasingly significant, the traceability of AI-processed image data has become critical to ensuring research reproducibility, data reusability, and workflow auditability. However, in biodiversity image collections, persistent identifiers are still primarily limited to original specimens. Derived images generated through AI pipelines lack systematic provenance tracking, and their chain of lineage is broken once the data leaves the repository. This talk presents FishAIR's provenance model as a case study of how a production biodiversity image system extends persistent identifiers beyond original specimens to AI-derived images, maintaining an unbroken chain from digitized collection images through bounding box, segmentation, and landmark processing. At the core of this model is the treatment of processing activities as citable first-class objects: each “batch” representing a set of image processing runs is treated as a traceable workflow event. It is assigned a unique ARK identifier recording the responsible institution, pipeline type, software configuration, and parameters. This design ensures that provenance information is not merely optional metadata but an inherent property of every derived image, without relying on external workflow management infrastructure. By maintaining this chain, FishAIR enables data users to trace the origin and transformation history of any training image and identify which processing stage or source collections those images originated from when model performance varies across different data subsets. The framework further supports transparent and auditable AI biodiversity workflows by preserving lineage across all stages of image derivation and reuse.

actual.identification_notes: Moved from sixth to third slot: the convener said the scheduled third speaker (Sefika Efeoglu) could not make it and a team member would present. The talk appears to be pre-recorded or remote ('It's online'); speaker introduced as 'Xiaojing Wang' from 'Turin University' (ASR for Tulane). ASR renders Fish-AIR as 'FishR/Fishare/Fish Share' and ARK IDs as 'ArchIDs'. Yasin Bakış and Henk Bart offered to take questions; none were asked.

content_items.summary: Xiaojun Wang presented how the Fish-AIR repository records provenance for AI-derived fish images produced mostly by external pipelines. Fish-AIR holds just over 400,000 source images from 67 institutions plus about 306,000 derived images (bounding boxes, segmentations, landmarks), and each derived record carries a parent ARK (its direct input image) and a batch ARK (the processing run), so following parent links reconstructs lineage back to the specimen image. Batch records (a class with 14 terms in the Fish-AIR vocabulary) store shared run metadata once, and ARKs, parent and batch references travel in exported CSV and RDF downloads. Automated checks of about 359,000 parent links and 763,000 batch links found all resolvable, enabling researchers to trace odd results and compare model performance across collections or batches.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Two persistent-identifier links per derived image, parent and batch, are enough to preserve auditable lineage and pipeline context for AI-processed biodiversity images, even outside the repository.
content_items.why_it_matters: As AI pipelines generate derived media at scale, lineage that survives export is essential for reproducibility and for diagnosing whether model errors come from source material or processing.
key_points: Fish-AIR serves the Biology-Guided Neural Networks and Imageomics projects; derived outputs are produced mostly by external teams' pipelines.

Snapshot: just over 400,000 source image records from 67 institutions and 7 source collections; about 306,000 derived images, including roughly 290,000 bounding box images, 42,000 segmentations and 27,000 landmark images.
A specimen image can pass through bounding box, segmentation and landmark tasks; each output is a separate record in a separate batch, and file names cannot preserve relationships.
Each record has its own ARK; derived images also store a parent ARK and a batch ARK; source images have no parent, and harvested images reference harvest batches.

21 batch records describe AI pipeline runs by the Tulane and Virginia Tech teams; batch is a class with 14 terms (pipeline, institution, creator, project, date, supplement path, code repository, etc.).
The largest batch contains almost a quarter of a million outputs; shared metadata is stored once on the batch record.
Downloads include multimedia and batch CSVs with ARKs, citation information, term definitions and an RDF model (Fish-AIR vocabulary version 3).
Link integrity checks run after each ingest and before every export; an early audit's 29 unresolved batch links all came from test records.
datasets: Fish-AIR source and derived fish images

notable_claims.claim: Automated checks of about 359,000 parent links and 763,000 batch links found all pointing to existing records, with no image as its own parent.
The exported files carry the parent chain and batch references, so users do not need access to the internal database to reconstruct relationships.

recommendations: Record for every derived image both its direct input image and its processing run with persistent identifiers.
results_findings: Full link integrity in the production database; the only unresolved links were in test records.
examples_case_studies: Fish-AIR AI processing chain: bounding box to segmentation to landmarks

representative_excerpt.text: To summarize, Fish Share uses ArchID to keep two parts of a provenance together, the image lineage and the pipeline context. The parent chain records the lineage, while the batch records provide the context.

Parent and batch ARK design.
Link integrity audit results.
