content_items.title: Unifying Biodiversity Images: Content-Based Identification with the ISCC standard (ISO 24138:2024)

programme.title: Unifying Biodiversity Images: Content-Based Identification with the ISCC standard (ISO 24138:2024)
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Digital images are vital to modern biodiversity science for e.g. studying specimens, identifying species, and extracting data by AI. However, sharing imagery faces critical challenges: image duplication across repositories, broken data links during reformatting, and AI-generated fakes undermining trust. Traditional PIDs (like DOIs) manage location but ignore content, while standard hashes (SHA-256) break with any pixel modification.

This presentation introduces the International Standard Content Code (ISCC, ISO 24138:2024) as a content-aware verification layer. The ISCC-CODE functions as a digital fingerprint derived from visual media, enabling similarity-based matching so that cropped, compressed, or converted images retain highly similar codes.

Because the code only describes the media itself, the ISCC Discovery Protocol (IDP) is proposed by T. Pan & M. Etzrodt (ISCC Foundation) to enable content-based discovery and provenance. The core of IDP is the Declaration Event - a FAIR Digital Object (FDO) identifying who declared what content at what time via a persistent ISCC-ID. Reference implementation: https://github.com/iscc/iscc-hub.

The IDP solves three critical problems:

Automated Deduplication: Content based clustering of identical or near-identical images across infrastructures without relying on inconsistent metadata. Annotation Resilience: Keeping downstream annotations anchored to an image even when it is manipulated across workflows. AI Fake Detection & Provenance: Using cryptographically signed Declaration Events to verify the origin and authenticity of images, isolating synthetic fakes.

A content-derived fingerprint implementation like IDP offers a scalable, decentralized path to securing trust and interoperability in biodiversity imagery.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Wouter Edding' (ASR). ASR occasionally renders ISCC as 'ICC', SHA-256 as 'SHA-2056' and Hugging Face as 'Hackingface'. Affiliation not stated in the recording.

content_items.summary: Wouter Addink introduced the International Standard Content Code (ISCC, ISO 24138:2024) as a content-aware identifier for biodiversity media; nobody in the room had heard of it. He explained why DOIs (location-focused) and cryptographic hashes (break on any pixel, metadata or format change) fall short for images, and how ISCC combines meta, content, data and instance codes so that content codes survive watermarks or format conversion and Hamming distance measures similarity. A beta 'declaration event' binds an ISCC to a signed creator and timestamp using DIDs and an append-only log run on decentralised hubs, enabling content-based discovery, provenance, isolation of AI fakes and annotations resilient to derivatives.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: ISCC gives images a content-derived, similarity-comparable identifier that anyone can recompute, addressing duplication, broken links and AI-generated fakes.
content_items.why_it_matters: Biodiversity media are copied, converted and increasingly faked; a content-based identifier could keep annotations and provenance attached across copies and formats.
key_points: Challenges: AI-generated fakes undermining trust, uncoordinated copies, and metadata/provenance lost when files are renamed or converted.
PIDs like DOIs, RORs and ORCIDs work where identifying metadata is easy, but images need their content to distinguish them.
Standard hashes such as SHA-256 change completely with any pixel, metadata or format change.
ISCC works for images, video, audio and text; a full code concatenates meta, content, data and instance units (typically 64 bits each) with self-describing header (main type, subtype).
The instance code behaves like a hash; the data code changes with data changes; the content code stays the same under format conversion or watermarking.
Because ISCC codes carry semantics, Hamming distance between codes measures how different two items are, enabling similarity matching.
Declaration events (beta, not yet in the standard) bind an ISCC to a signature and timestamp as a FAIR Digital Object, using DIDs and an append-only log on self-hostable hubs rather than blockchain.
Codes can be generated locally from content; start with the Hugging Face playground, then the Python software and possibly a local registry node.

notable_claims.claim: Standard hashes such as SHA-256 change completely if even one pixel, the metadata or the file format changes.
The ISCC content code stays the same when an image's format changes or a watermark is added, while the data code changes.
Declaration events can isolate AI-generated fakes because fakes will not carry a signature of who created the content.

recommendations: Link annotations to ISCC codes rather than image files so they persist across derivatives.
limitations: Declaration events are still in beta and not part of the standard; the speaker was not involved in the standard and does not know all details.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether the code is stored in a separate catalogue or embedded, e.g. in EXIF.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Either; it can go in EXIF, but since anyone can recreate it from the content it will mainly be kept in a separate catalogue.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether the content embedding algorithm is fixed (like CLIP) or selectable.
q_and_a.answer_summary: It is fixed per media type, with different algorithms for images, sound (via a sonogram) and video; details are in the online documentation.

q_and_a.question: Yasin Bakış asked how provenance works when multiple sources create the same object.
q_and_a.answer_summary: There can be only one creator: whoever declares it with their cryptographic key is the originator; the rest are copies.

representative_excerpt.text: So usually you say if you have a persistent identifier, you don't want any semantics in it. This carries semantics. And I think it's fine because it's identifying the content itself.

notable_moments.description: Show of hands: nobody knew ISCC.
The four ISCC units and why the content code survives format changes.
Declaration events binding creator and timestamp.

content_items.title: Robot-ready by construction: an ontology-driven, SHACL-validated submission pipeline for national ecological monitoring data

programme.title: Robot-ready by construction: an ontology-driven, SHACL-validated submission pipeline for national ecological monitoring data
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
Some approaches to robot-ready biodiversity data work backwards: collect first, then retrofit standards-compliant metadata before submission. The Ecological Monitoring System Australia (EMSA) takes the opposite approach. Its Monitor platform captures field data across 38 ecological survey protocols, and the export pipeline emits standards-aligned RDF at source - so submissions arrive at the national Biodiversity Data Repository (BDR) robot-ready by construction, not by remediation.

The pipeline resolves every attribute, property, and observation-procedure URI live against EMSA vocabularies in a GraphDB SPARQL endpoint, with caching and vocabulary harmonisation mapping field terms to controlled vocabularies. Data quality is enforced at both boundaries: JSON Schema validation governs what enters the system from the field, and per-protocol SHACL shapes gate what leaves - submissions that fail validation are not exported. Provenance is tracked end-to-end from field collection through to BDR ingest, and a companion XLSX gives curators a human-readable view of what the machine submitted. The full pipeline is config-driven, containerised, and reproducible.

We discuss what works well - SPARQL resolution keeps the pipeline aligned as vocabularies evolve, and SHACL gating catches structural errors before they reach BDR curators - and the practical lessons of maintaining a config-driven exporter across 38 protocols as both the monitoring program and its target vocabularies continue to grow.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual (pre-recorded) talk. ASR renders the speaker as 'Andrew Topnakov' and TERN as 'Turing'. He presents for the team and credits Waleed (ASR 'Walid Alnam') with building the exporter. EMSA and ABIS are rendered correctly for the most part.

content_items.summary: Andrew Tokmakoff described how TERN Ecosystem Surveillance moved from a decade-old Android app and Postgres database to EMSA (Ecological Monitoring System Australia), built for the federal government, where a single data model specification drives both the offline-capable field app (a PWA) and the exporter that pushes RDF to Australia's national Biodiversity Data Repository. Protocol steps and attributes are mapped to IRIs, an OpenAPI 3.0 specification generates UI elements (e.g. lookup-table references) and validates JSON on the way in, and the exporter maps flat JSON into the graph-based ABIS and TERN ontologies, resolving vocabularies live via SPARQL and validating output with SHACL shapes. Data therefore arrive 'robot-ready by construction' rather than by later remediation.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Driving both field data capture and RDF export from one semantically annotated specification makes monitoring data standards-compliant and machine-ready from the start.
content_items.why_it_matters: It demonstrates a working alternative to retrofitting standards onto legacy data: specification-driven collection with validation at both boundaries, feeding a national biodiversity knowledge graph.
key_points: TERN is Australia's national terrestrial ecosystem research infrastructure (funded through NCRIS); Ecosystem Surveillance, based in Adelaide since 2011, runs a long-term standardised plot network, mainly in the rangelands.
Legacy system: AusScribe Android app, Postgres and CouchDB; new system: EMSA protocols and software, with a PWA field app and a Strapi headless CMS back end ('Core') on Postgres.
Two routes to standards-compliant data: collect first and map later, or, as with EMSA, start from protocol definitions that drive both collection and RDF creation.
Data are structured surveys, not just occurrences; protocol steps and procedures are mapped to IRIs, making data self-describing.

An OpenAPI 3.0 specification (close to JSON Schema) is a machine-readable contract: the app builds its UI from it (e.g. an x-lutRef veg growth form lookup) and the exporter reads the same key to map codes into the graph.

The exporter maps flat JSON to graph models (ABIS national profile, TERN ontologies, EMSA protocol-specific SHACL shapes), resolving EMSA vocabularies via SPARQL against GraphDB with caching, so it adapts as protocols evolve.
Quality gating at both boundaries: JSON Schema validation in the app and on submission; SHACL validation of RDF on export.
In the national Biodiversity Data Repository, shared IRIs let queries walk from TERN plot observations to other providers' records without complex mapping.
datasets: TERN Ecosystem Surveillance plot network data

notable_claims.claim: In EMSA a single data model specification informs both the field client and the exporter that pushes data to the national Biodiversity Data Repository.
Shared IRIs let queries walk from TERN plot observations to other providers' records in the BDR without complex mapping.
Because the exporter queries EMSA vocabularies dynamically, it should accommodate protocol changes relatively flexibly.

recommendations: Attach meaning wherever it is known and validate both on the way in and on the way out.
future_work: Possible future uses include generating new front ends from the OpenAPI spec, graph-wide querying, habitat/condition classification, and LLM proposals checked by SHACL verifiers.
examples_case_studies: TERN point-intercept vegetation protocol (growth form lookup)

representative_excerpt.text: But with EMSA, we've gone the other way and we start with the protocol definition, which drives the field app collection, and it also drives the RDF creation. Which we then validate, and then we make sure that that's all good before it goes into the repository.

notable_moments.description: System overview: one specification informs client and exporter.
Point-intercept example with a lookup-table reference used by both UI and exporter.
Quality gating at both boundaries with JSON Schema and SHACL.

content_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Amplifies Paleontology's Reproducibility Problem

programme.title: Artificial Intelligence Amplifies Paleontology’s Reproducibility Problem
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract: Paleontology has become a data-intensive science. Along with the specimen, large amounts of associated data are produced. These data are distributed across supplementary files, institutional databases, and discipline-specific repositories, and reproducibility problems are common: missing datasets, character matrices that fail to execute, incomplete documentation, unverifiable specimen vouchers, and missing methodological detail. Many of these problems predate AI, but AI methods are now being applied to paleontological data faster than existing infrastructure was designed to support, particularly LLMs that extract structured data from legacy literature and vision models that classify specimens from images. AI offers reproducibility benefits, including standardization at scale and recovery of data from inaccessible literature. However, it also introduces a specific risk: it can scale and conceal existing data quality problems by converting incomplete, ambiguous, or unverifiable source material into structured outputs that meet FAIR criteria and appear authoritative. A dataset can pass automated validation, receive a persistent identifier, and be reused in computational workflows while lacking the provenance, expert validation, and traceable interpretation required to assess its reliability. AI-readiness in paleontology must therefore be defined by verifiability, including provenance to source evidence, executability of analyses, and traceability of expert judgment. Journals should require disclosure of AI involvement in dataset construction and extend peer review to AI-generated data; repositories should treat AI provenance, validation status, and source linkage as first-class metadata.

actual.identification_notes: Virtual (pre-recorded video) talk played after a search for the uploaded files; speaker introduced as 'Brooke Longfox'. Co-authored with Mark Young, editor-in-chief of Historical Biology. The talk title is phrased as a question ('Is Artificial Intelligence Amplifying...?').

content_items.summary: Brooke Long-Fox, a data curation scientist at MorphoBank and data editor for Historical Biology, argued that AI is entering a field that already has reproducibility problems of availability (data not deposited or on personal websites), documentation (no README, undefined characters) and traceability (unclear links from evidence to result). AI can turn ambiguous or incomplete sources into perfectly formatted, schema-valid tables that get DOIs and feed further AI, improving structure without improving scientific validity. Using morphological character matrices, she showed that a binary score can encode expert judgements about homology, preservation and ontogeny, and proposed adding verifiability to AI readiness: tracing assertions to evidence, recording whether they were transcribed, transformed or inferred, and who validated them.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: AI can make uncertain paleontological data look clean and authoritative, so AI-ready data must also be verifiable back to evidence and interpretation.
content_items.why_it_matters: It distinguishes technical validity from scientific validity, a warning relevant to any biodiversity data being mass-extracted or inferred by AI.
key_points: This is not an argument against AI; she uses AI-assisted curation, but AI can amplify existing reproducibility problems.
Paleontology is data-intensive; the digital extended specimen links a specimen to images, occurrences, stratigraphy, measurements, matrices and outputs, so errors propagate further.
Availability problems: data never deposited, manuscripts claiming no data exist, files on personal websites or cloud links, private or incomplete repository records.
Documentation problems: no README or data dictionary, unexplained abbreviations, 3D models without links to specimens, incomplete character definitions; a PID says where a file is, not what it means.
Traceability problems: data statements not matching deposits, scores not linked to sources, matrices modified across studies without documentation, unclear versions.
AI can produce schema-valid, DOI-bearing structured outputs from ambiguous sources (e.g. OCR column shifts, inconsistent translation), which then feed other AI systems.
Technical validity is not scientific validity: a matrix cell such as character 37 = 0/1 may encode reasoning about homology, absence vs non-preservation, ontogeny, polymorphism or inapplicability.
AI-ready data should be machine-readable, FAIR, documented and validated, and for interpretive data also verifiable.
questions: Can current standards record that an assertion was generated by AI-assisted inference and then confirmed by a domain expert?

notable_claims.claim: AI can transform incomplete or ambiguous information into structured outputs that look ready for reuse, even passing schema validation and receiving a DOI.
Character states in morphological matrices can encode expert judgement rather than simple observations waiting to be extracted.

recommendations: Define the use case (extracting, transforming or inferring).
Preserve source, method, responsible agent, validation status and uncertainty.
Crosswalk existing standards such as Darwin Core and identify gaps.
examples_case_studies: MorphoBank skull image with specimen, photo and character-state information
Historical Biology journal data policy experience

representative_excerpt.text: So the structure has been improved, but the underlying scientific uncertainty has not necessarily improved with it. So that is the distinction I want to make between technical validity and scientific validity.

notable_moments.description: Three categories of existing reproducibility problems.
The failure mode: AI makes uncertainty look structured.
Morphological character matrix example.
Practical path toward verifiable robot-ready data.

content_items.title: AI Ready Standards with Croissant for Type Specimens Catalog Datasets

programme.title: AI Ready Standards with Croissant for Type Specimens Catalog Datasets
programme.session: SYM46 AI-Readiness Metrics and Metadata for Biodiversity Data
programme.abstract:
The FAIR principles are fundamental to Open Science. Publishing datasets used in Artificial Intelligence (AI) experiments in accordance with these principles is essential for ensuring reproducibility. Additionally, these FAIR datasets enhance the performance of Machine Learning (ML) applications, e.g., species labeling using named entity recognition models. Recently, ML Commons introduced Croissant, an ML-ready dataset format designed for seamless integration with ML models and with ML-ready dataset-sharing platforms such as Hugging Face.

Biodiversity data mobilization necessitates adherence to FAIR principles that go beyond merely sharing data in structured formats. We present an experimental approach to converting unstructured text from entomological type specimen catalogs into Darwin Core (DwC) metadata using Large Language Models, including GPT and Qwen. Subsequently, we map Croissant metadata fields to DwC terms-such as dwc:genus, dwc:scientificName, and dwc:individualCount-because these terms can be used to make type specimen catalogs machine-readable.

To evaluate whether our datasets align with FAIR principles for ML, we generate and conduct experiments on subsets of them. These metadata are then integrated into the NFDI4DataScience metadata portal, where FAIR metrics are visualized using the Piveau metric service. This portal provides metadata on datasets for AI use and metrics on FAIR principles. Complementing this quantitative assessment, we validate our metadata format using the FAIR Checker service.

Our proposed metadata framework for type specimen catalogs serves as a reference model for broader applications within biodiversity research domains. In addition, we provide a standardized protocol for the open mobilization of entomological type specimen data.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded video played last, although scheduled third (the convener said earlier the third speaker could not make it). She presents the work with Jana Hofmann from Senckenberg.

content_items.summary: Sefika Efeoglu presented a workflow for turning historical type specimen catalogues into AI-ready datasets: LLMs (e.g. GPT and Qwen) extract structured information from unstructured catalogue text, which is expressed in Darwin Core and then described with ML Commons Croissant metadata in JSON-LD. She showed how Darwin Core fields map to Croissant fields (scientific name as label, genus as taxonomic feature, individual count as integer, catalogue number as identifier, locality, event date, collector, type status) and how the pipeline evaluates FAIR metrics. The approach aims to bridge biodiversity standards and ML dataset platforms such as Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Combining LLM extraction, Darwin Core and Croissant metadata offers a route from historical specimen catalogues to FAIR, ML-ready datasets.
content_items.why_it_matters: Croissant is becoming the metadata layer ML platforms understand; mapping Darwin Core into it could make collection data directly discoverable and loadable in ML ecosystems.
key_points: Biodiversity data are used for species identification, named entity recognition, taxonomic knowledge extraction and knowledge graphs, but historical catalogues are largely unstructured text.
FAIRness supports ML reproducibility, clarity, sharing and more reliable model development; the aim is to extend FAIR into ML workflows.

Croissant (ML Commons) is a standardised, machine-readable metadata format for ML-ready datasets supported by platforms such as Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML: 'create once, publish anywhere, use everywhere'.
Workflow: type specimen catalogue, unstructured text, LLM-assisted extraction (GPT, Qwen), Darwin Core metadata, Croissant metadata, AI-ready dataset.

Mapping examples: scientificName as label for classification, genus as taxonomic feature, individualCount as integer feature, catalogNumber as unique identifier, locality, eventDate, collector (provenance) and typeStatus.
Records are represented in Croissant JSON-LD with explicit field data types; the pipeline measures FAIR metrics and metadata quality.
methods: schema mapping Darwin Core to Croissant

notable_claims.claim: The workflow transforms type specimen catalogue text via LLM extraction into Darwin Core and then Croissant metadata to produce an AI-ready dataset.
Mapping to Croissant preserves Darwin Core semantics rather than discarding them.

recommendations: Use Croissant as a common metadata layer to connect biodiversity standards with the ML ecosystem.
future_work: Extend the approach to other biodiversity collections.

representative_excerpt.text: The point is not to discard the Darwin Core. Instead, it preserves its biodiverse semantics and expresses those elements with a metadata structure that ML systems can understand.

notable_moments.description: Proposed workflow from catalogue text to AI-ready dataset.
Darwin Core to Croissant field mapping.

content_items.title: Not just another database: building the future of freshwater taxonomy with FADAtims

programme.title: Not just another database: building the future of freshwater taxonomy with FADAtims
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: Freshwater biodiversity is declining rapidly, yet freshwater taxonomy remains fragmented across databases, standards and expert communities. Maintaining reliable species lists is challenging because names change continuously, new taxa are described, and taxonomic concepts differ between regions and organism groups. These issues limit interoperability between biodiversity infrastructures and constrain large-scale ecological assessments and policy applications. To address this gap, we are developing FADAtims, an online taxonomic information management system for collaborative curation of freshwater biodiversity checklists, which is developed within the Belspo-funded infraFADA project. The platform enables registered experts to curate and continuously update species names, synonyms, classification, distribution and status information through a transparent and traceable workflow. FADAtims is designed as a FAIR, interoperable and machine-actionable infrastructure component for freshwater biodiversity data. Built with open-source technologies and aligned with Biodiversity Information Standards, it supports data exchange with major biodiversity infrastructures including GBIF, Catalogue of Life and the Freshwater Information Platform. Interoperability with systems such as WoRMS and TaxonWorks further supports harmonisation and long-term sustainability. The platform aims to provide an authoritative freshwater taxonomic backbone that can be linked to occurrence, trait and monitoring databases as well as conservation assessments. We present the current status of FADAtims, its role within the emerging freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem and discuss community-driven approaches for sustaining curated freshwater taxonomy infrastructures.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Astrid Schmidt-Gloeble'/'Gloeble' (ASR) together with 'Geraldine Mertens', manager of the InfraFADA project, who presented the FADA history section (05:59:39-06:06:26); Geraldine's surname spelling is uncertain. ASR renders FADAtims as 'FADA Teams/FADA-TiMS' and Lasiotiphula-type genus names inconsistently.

content_items.summary: Astrid Schmidt-Kloiber opened with a caddisfly whose accepted name differs between the Trichoptera World Checklist, GBIF/Catalogue of Life and freshwaterecology.info, arguing freshwater biodiversity has a taxonomy problem rather than a database shortage. Geraldine Mertens recounted how the original Freshwater Animal Diversity Assessment produced species lists and a Hydrobiologia special issue but then stagnated, and how the InfraFADA project rebuilt an expert consortium (over 100 experts, 61 animal groups plus macrophytes) with exchanges from WoRMS and TaxonWorks. Astrid then demonstrated FADAtims, the operational curation system with role-based permissions, bulk upload, detail pages linked to GBIF and the IUCN Red List, and exports including DOI-versioned checklists via ChecklistBank, and raised sustainability of people, infrastructure and interoperability.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: FADAtims turns the dormant FADA checklists into a living, expert-curated and interoperable freshwater taxonomic infrastructure, but its future depends on sustaining experts and systems.
content_items.why_it_matters: Consistent freshwater taxonomy underpins occurrence integration, Red List assessment and ecological analysis; FADAtims is intended as the backbone for several freshwater portals.
key_points: Example: Lepidostoma basale is accepted in the Trichoptera World Checklist and freshwaterecology.info but treated as a synonym in GBIF and Catalogue of Life.
Freshwater biodiversity has 'not a database shortage, but rather a taxonomy problem'.

FADA started over 20 years ago; its expert lists and a Hydrobiologia special issue were produced, but maintenance stopped when funding ended due to technology limits and poor machine-to-machine exchange.

InfraFADA rebuilt the expert consortium: over 100 experts, 61 animal groups plus a macrophyte chapter; 43 Excel templates (24 received, 19 in progress), with 15 lists expected from WoRMS and 3 from TaxonWorks.

FADAtims supports role-based permissions (expert, expert leader, group member, public), bulk upload, search and filters, and detail pages with taxonomy, environmental information, references and links to GBIF occurrences and the IUCN Red List.
Experts curate names, synonyms, classification, authorships, FADA environmental regions and distribution; edits are tracked.
Exports include PDFs, CSV and versioned checklists that receive DOIs through ChecklistBank via ColDP packages; DOIs are the main incentive for experts.

FADAtims harvests from and links back to WoRMS and TaxonWorks, delivers to Catalogue of Life (and thus GBIF), and will serve as backbone for the FIP data portal and FBIS; a GBIF freshwater tag is still missing.
FADA More, a three-year follow-up, will maintain and enrich data (molecular data, cryptic diversity, parasites and hosts, ecological information).
questions: Who curates, keeps experts engaged and replaces retiring experts?
Who maintains the database and mappings between systems, and keeps exchange aligned with evolving standards?

notable_claims.claim: The same caddisfly species has different accepted names in the Trichoptera World Checklist, GBIF/Catalogue of Life and freshwaterecology.info.
More than 100 experts worldwide are updating FADA lists covering 61 animal groups plus macrophytes.
A DOI for their versioned checklist is the main incentive for contributing scientists.

recommendations: Focus on interoperability and interconnection rather than new databases.
Share development and maintenance through multi-tenant community infrastructures.
limitations: FADAtims lists for some groups are still being updated; a freshwater tag in GBIF is still missing.
future_work: Link to freshwaterecology.info and the Red List database.
FADA More: add molecular data, cryptic diversity, parasites and host relationships, and ecological information.

representative_excerpt.text: So the future of freshwater biodiversity data depends not on more databases, but on better interconnectedness and interoperability.

notable_moments.description: Caddisfly naming conflict across databases.
FADAtims interface walk-through.
Sustainability challenges for people, infrastructure and interoperability.

content_items.title: Catalogue of Life and Freshwater species data

programme.title: Catalogue of Life and Freshwater species data
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: 30 years ago the activities that led to the Catalogue of Life started. For 25 years the catalogue of described organisms of all life, has been freely available online. GBIF, also celebrating a 25 year anniversary, is now making use of the Catalogue of Life as the taxonomic reference for the 3.7 billion species occurrences it mediates. Although a lot of progress has been made, there are still obvious taxonomic gaps. Some groups are notoriously under-represented and incomplete (like insects). In other cases, taxonomic data from specific ecosystem realms like freshwater is scarce. The Catalogue of Life infrastructure, ChecklistBank, now promotes the open data publishing of taxonomic and nomenclatural resources, and different types of species lists (such as policy-relevant lists). The infrastructure also provides the means to share species interaction data. We will provide an overview of the available information in Catalogue of Life and in its infrastructure. We also discuss how this data could be improved, for example through collaboration with initiatives like the Freshwater Animal Diversity Assessment.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Olaf Beunke' (ASR) with collaborators Diana Hernandez and Camila Plata. He could not see his PDF slides on the lectern. Acknowledges colleague 'Yuri Raskov' (Yuri Roskov).

content_items.summary: Olaf Banki marked 25 years of the public Catalogue of Life (over 2.2 million accepted species) and described ChecklistBank, its API-first infrastructure with around 65,000 data sources, including about 1,000 national lists, 400 invasive species lists and 200 global lists. He admitted CoL cannot currently tell which species are freshwater: WoRMS provides freshwater/marine/brackish/terrestrial flags that CoL holds but cannot model or show, lists like freshwaterecology.info are not yet published there, AlgaeBase is not openly licensed, and FADA's 2013 lists are outdated. He pledged that within about a year CoL will ingest FADAtims data and add freshwater, brackish, water-dependent and aquatic designations to its systems and API, which would flow to GBIF.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Catalogue of Life pledges to model and expose freshwater designations within a year, fed by FADAtims and WoRMS, finally allowing freshwater species and occurrences to be identified via GBIF.
content_items.why_it_matters: Because CoL is GBIF's taxonomic reference, adding habitat designations would solve a 15-year-old problem of analysing freshwater biodiversity from aggregated data.
key_points: 2026 is the 25th year of public CoL releases; activities began in 1996. The release has slightly more than 2.2 million accepted species.
CoL now publishes a base release and an extended release adding e.g. Plazi publications, UNITE species hypotheses and Barcode of Life.
ChecklistBank is an open repository for taxonomic, nomenclatural and policy lists, hosts CoL's assembly tooling and comparison tools; all functionality is in the API.
About 65,000 data sources in ChecklistBank, growing monthly mostly through publications from Plazi and Pensoft; roughly 1,000 national lists, 400 invasive species lists and 200 global lists.
CoL cannot yet filter freshwater species in its own product; freshwaterecology.info matches well except phytobenthos but is not published in ChecklistBank.
WoRMS flags marine/freshwater/brackish/terrestrial but CoL cannot model this in its front end; algae coverage is weak because AlgaeBase is not openly licensed.
Four FADA lists from the 2013 assessment remain in CoL and have not been updated; about 1,700 datasets mention freshwater in their title, mostly Plazi publications.

Pledge: connect to FADAtims (which already exports CoL data packages) and add freshwater, brackish, water-dependent and aquatic designations to CoL systems and API within about a year, flowing to GBIF.

notable_claims.claim: The Catalogue of Life release has slightly more than 2.2 million accepted species.
ChecklistBank holds about 65,000 data sources, including about 1,000 national species lists, 400 invasive species lists and 200 global lists.
Catalogue of Life cannot currently determine which species in its product are freshwater.
CoL expects to integrate freshwater, brackish, water-dependent and aquatic designations into its systems and API within about a year.

recommendations: Publish freshwater species lists to ChecklistBank so they can be evaluated and integrated.
results_findings: Matching freshwaterecology.info and WoRMS against CoL shows good coverage for most groups except phytobenthos and algae.
limitations: Algae are poorly covered because AlgaeBase is not openly licensed.
FADA lists in CoL date from 2013.
future_work: Ingest updated FADAtims lists.
Model and expose habitat designations in CoL and its API.

representative_excerpt.text: So this is our pledge in this collaboration that we would solve that problem. And so next year, if we haven't done it, then let's do it.

notable_moments.description: ChecklistBank data source statistics.
Admission that CoL cannot yet identify freshwater species.

content_items.title: A species-level taxonomic catalog of Neotropical freshwater insects: building a consensus reference for occurrence data integration and conservation planning

programme.title: A species-level taxonomic catalog of Neotropical freshwater insects: building a consensus reference for occurrence data integration, and conservation planning.
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: Freshwaters are among the most biodiverse yet data-deficient habitats globally, and the Neotropical region exemplifies this paradox - exceptional aquatic insect diversity combined with critical taxonomic and distributional gaps rooted in historical undersampling. To our knowledge, no equivalent species-level, multi-order catalog of freshwater insects exists for the Neotropical region. Here we present an ongoing effort to compile a DarwinCore-compliant catalog of freshwater aquatic insects for the Neotropical lowlands, covering seven orders: Trichoptera, Coleoptera, Odonata, Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, Hemiptera, and Megaloptera. All compiled species names are verified against the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy and the Catalogue of Life, documenting nomenclatural discrepancies including synonyms, combinationes novae, and typographic errors. Country-level distribution data are linked to georeferenced occurrence records from GBIF and regional sources. For each verified species, occurrence records are cleaned and linked to stream network segments, with environmental and topographic variables extracted at the sub-catchment scale. This dataset will underpin distribution modelling across the Magdalena-Cauca Basin in Colombia, assessing how river network structure shapes richness, rarity, and endemism, and prioritising conservation areas accounting for cumulative hydropower impacts on freshwater connectivity.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Alejandra Correa Botella from Colombia' (ASR). A PhD student; affiliation not stated. Some taxon names are garbled by ASR (e.g. 'Anachroneura nolicoda', 'Owatometra uesa'). The moderator described this as a student project.

content_items.summary: Alejandra Correa-Bedoya presented a Darwin Core-compliant species-level checklist of seven orders of freshwater insects for the Neotropics (southern Mexico to Brazil), compiled over six months for her PhD. She showed that names documented for Colombia (about 1,250 species) often have no occurrence records there, due to taxonomic resolution bias and a data supply gap rather than platform failures, verified names against global infrastructures, and noted her list triples known Odonata species for Colombia compared with a national effort. Grounding it in the free-flowing Samaná Norte river, threatened by planned dams and invasive species, she argued that without species names there are no occurrences, no species distribution models and no evidence for protecting rivers.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Without a reliable species-level checklist, Neotropical freshwater insect occurrences, distribution models and conservation arguments cannot be built.
content_items.why_it_matters: It links taxonomic infrastructure directly to conservation decisions under dam development pressure in one of the world's most biodiverse and data-deficient regions.
key_points: Global freshwater populations declined about 83% since 1970 (Living Planet), about 95% in Latin America and the Caribbean; Central and South America are data-deficient hotspots.
Dam expansion is concentrated on the Andean slopes, modifying flows before data exist to assess losses.
The checklist covers seven orders from southern Mexico to Brazil, excluding the southern cone as a distinct biogeographic region; Coleoptera and Diptera are richest.
It is a taxon-core list (names, synonyms, classification) of officially described species, the naming backbone needed before occurrence data can be resolved.
Colombia has the most documented species of these orders (about 1,250), reflecting its position among heterogeneous biogeographic subregions.
Example stonefly: GBIF shows records across its range but none in Colombia at the range centre, indicating nobody has named and looked for it there.

Verification against GBIF found flags such as recent nomenclatural changes (Coleoptera), typographic/algorithmic errors (Trichoptera) and a genus reassignment (Hemiptera); she frames this as a data supply gap, not a platform problem.
In the Samaná Norte basin, about 600 occurrence records of these orders resolve only to genus, which is not interpretable for conservation decisions.

limitations: Includes only described species; many genera lack reliable species-level information.
future_work: Use the checklist for species distribution models and spatial prioritisation in the Magdalena basin.

content_items.title: Biodiversity data at your fingertips: open-access freshwater biodiversity information systems for South Africa and Africa

programme.title: Biodiversity data at your fingertips: open-access freshwater biodiversity information systems for South Africa and Africa
programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: Freshwater biodiversity data are essential for monitoring ecosystem change, informing conservation, and supporting evidence-based management. However, such data often remain fragmented, inaccessible, or poorly integrated across scales, institutions, and regions. The Freshwater Biodiversity Information System (FBIS) and FBIS-Africa platforms, developed for South Africa and the broader African region respectively, respond directly to this need. FBIS is a powerful, visual, data-rich system designed to host, share, and explore freshwater biodiversity data. Its design and functionality have been shaped by key user groups, including water resource managers, conservation practitioners, planners, researchers, and environmental consultants. Both platforms interoperate with global biodiversity infrastructures, including GBIF and the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, contributing to a more connected and accessible freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem. By combining regional expertise, open infrastructure, and interoperable data workflows, FBIS and FBIS-Africa demonstrate how community-driven information systems can support FAIR biodiversity data mobilisation and translate knowledge into actionable conservation and management outcomes. The South African platform already supports improved freshwater science, conservation, and decision-making at a national scale, with approximately 14 million occurrence records across eight biodiversity modules. The recently developed FBIS-Africa platform is rapidly expanding in both data coverage and user uptake. Together, these platforms play a critical role in translating freshwater biodiversity data into informed monitoring, management, and conservation action across local, regional, continental, and global scales.

content_items.summary: Helen Dallas presented FBIS, the Freshwater Biodiversity Information System for South Africa, and its continental scale-up FBIS-Africa. Developed since 2017 through user-centred design for water resource and conservation managers, researchers, consultants and policymakers, FBIS holds over 14 million occurrence records across eight biodiversity modules and has 1,648 registered users. It uses the GBIF taxonomic backbone (with planned FADA integration), links to the IUCN Red List, offers spatial and temporal filters, spatial layers and standardised dashboards, and attaches citation metadata to every record. Separating the engine from the data enabled redeployment for other platforms via a multi-tenant model that improves sustainability.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Co-designed, open and interoperable freshwater information systems like FBIS turn fragmented records into decision-ready information, and multi-tenancy helps keep them sustainable.
content_items.why_it_matters: It offers a proven, reusable platform model for regional biodiversity data systems in resource-constrained settings.
key_points: Freshwater data are fragmented, inaccessible and poorly integrated, and thus underused in decision-making.
FBIS development began in 2017 with a user-centred approach, designing backwards from end users' needs.

Separating the engine from the data allowed redeployment for other, including non-freshwater, platforms and scale-up to FBIS-Africa.
Multi-tenant model: independent governance and branding per tenant, shared costs, shared improvements and increased resilience.
Five design principles: stakeholder co-design, interoperability (GBIF, IUCN), open access, sustained support and partnerships, and multi-tenancy.

notable_claims.claim: FBIS currently holds more than 14 million occurrence records of freshwater taxa.
FBIS has 1,648 registered users actively uploading and downloading data.
Every occurrence record on FBIS and FBIS-Africa has associated metadata for citation and attribution.

recommendations: Co-design with stakeholders, interoperate with global infrastructures, keep data open, secure sustained partnerships, and adopt multi-tenancy.
future_work: Integrate FBIS taxonomy with FADA.

representative_excerpt.text: In conclusion, open, interoperable, and user-driven biodiversity information systems can transform freshwater data into action.

content_items.title: The FIPbio data portal: towards an integrated freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem

programme.title: The FIPbio data portal: towards an integrated freshwater biodiversity data ecosystem

speakers.name: Vanessa Bremerich
speakers.affiliation: Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB)

programme.session: SYM37A A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract:
Freshwater biodiversity research, monitoring and policy increasingly rely on interoperable data infrastructures linking taxonomy, biodiversity observations, abiotic sampling data and remote sensing products. With the renewal of the freshwater biodiversity data portal FIPbio within the Freshwater Information Platform (FIP), we present a framework integrating freshwater occurrence records, eDNA observations, sampling data and satellite-derived environmental time series, including chlorophyll-a dynamics and land-use change, across lakes, wetlands and river catchmentsinto a unified freshwater data ecosystem.

The renewed portal builds on the Biodiversity Information Management System (BIMS), originally developed for the South African Freshwater Biodiversity Information System (FBIS). Central to FIPbio is the global Freshwater Animal Diversity Assessment (FADA) taxonomic backbone, continuously curated through the FADAtims platform. This freshwater-specific backbone enables a comprehensive overview of occurrence data mobilised through infrastructures such as GBIF.

Sampling sites are spatially linked to global freshwater environmental context layers including river networks, basins, lakes, wetlands and land-water interface classes. Occurrence records are automatically annotated with contextual dataset IDs and snapped to river network segments, enabling reproducible freshwater-specific analytical workflows using resources such as Hydrography90m.

FIPbio enhances the discoverability, interoperability and long-term reuse of freshwater biodiversity and monitoring data from local to global scales. The platform supports freshwater data mobilisation efforts, including those within the FWBON network and contributes to an integrated global freshwater biodiversity information landscape.

content_items.title: A collaborative perspective on a globally standardised river basin name database

programme.title: A collaborative perspective on a globally standardised river basin name database
programme.session: SYM37B A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract:
When categorising and aggregating data across a given landscape, Earth scientists tend to use grids, broad geographic delineations such as continents, or administrative units such as countries, counties or states. However, when the environmental characteristics and energy flows in a given region come into focus, then the drainage basin becomes an appropriate spatial unit. This is because of the topographic structure of the landscape along rivers, streams, lakes and wetlands that are laterally and longitudinally connected. Especially in light of global change, spatially pinpointing and being able to search a certain drainage basin by name - e.g. to analyse the observed and projected changes - represents a task that is important for the study of biodiversity as well as for neighbouring areas such as transnational water management. To date, though, a comprehensive and globally standardised resource of basin names is missing.

In this contribution, we will outline how such a resource could be developed, maintained and refined collaboratively on the basis of the Wikimedia and OpenStreetMap platforms and their respective communities. The Wikimedia ecosystem comprises of a suite of interconnected open collaborative platforms that already cover multiple facets of both river basins and biodiversity and that are multilingual. Wikidata in particular is a repository of semantic web-compatible general reference information whose entries include river basins, taxa, territorial entities, ecological concepts and scientific publications about any of these. Wikidata and its sister sites are also closely integrated with OpenStreetMap and citizen science efforts, and Wikidata identifiers are widely used in scholarly contexts and frequently mapped to entries in other relevant databases.

The speaker could not see or advance his PDF slides for the first minutes (07:56:02-07:57:35) and later spoke partly without them. Affiliation not stated.

content_items.summary: Daniel Mietchen argued that river basins are the natural spatial unit for freshwater biology but lack a global, multilingual naming system: geoscience grids and the Pfafstetter coding system ignore biology, naming, karst, flow changes and complex branching. Using Oslo's Akerselva as an example, he showed how Wikidata links the river, its drainage basin (Nordmarksvassdraget) and Norwegian REGINE and ELVIS identifiers, but that Wikidata's drainage basin statements are almost all Norwegian. He listed edge cases (seasonal and split rivers, karst, flow reversal, dams, historic courses and names, oral languages) and asked how TDWG groups, Wikidata and OpenStreetMap could collaborate, proposing an unconference session.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Freshwater biodiversity data need a global, multilingual, collaboratively maintained river basin naming system, and TDWG, Wikidata and OpenStreetMap could build it together.
content_items.why_it_matters: Being able to state in a standard way which river basin an occurrence belongs to would support freshwater invasions, connectivity and conservation analyses that grids cannot capture.

The Pfafstetter coding system is widely used in geodatabases but knows nothing about biology or names, and ignores karst, water level changes and complex branching.
The talk asks questions rather than giving answers: how can TDWG help express, e.g. in Darwin Core, that a fish record belongs to one basin and not another?
Akerselva example: basin delineation from AquaINFRA-style segment data, and Wikidata items linking river, source, mouth and drainage basin (Nordmarksvassdraget).
Norwegian identifiers exist (REGINE for basins, ELVIS for rivers); Wikidata has 431 items with drainage basin/REGINE statements and 1,066 with ELVIS IDs, almost all Norwegian.
Transboundary rivers carry names in several languages (e.g. Norway, Finland, Russia), raising the question of which to use.

Edge cases: seasonally dry or drought-split rivers, hunger stones, karst, seasonal flooding, flow reversal, groundwater, atmospheric rivers, paleohydrology, dams, historic courses and names, oral-only languages.
Candidate collaborators: relevant TDWG interest, task and maintenance groups; Wikidata; OpenStreetMap.

Which TDWG groups are relevant and active for this?
How to record an occurrence in an aquatic environment that changes over time?

Essentially all drainage basins with statements in Wikidata are from Norway.

recommendations: Start with main cases before edge cases.
Build on existing European work (WISE) and look at other regions.

content_items.title: From 'Lost in Translation' to Fit-for-Purpose Data: Why Ecologists and Conservation Practice Still Need Groupings and Uncertainties

programme.title: From “Lost in Translation” to Fit-for-Purpose Data: Why Ecologists and Conservation Practice Still Need groupings and cF
programme.session: SYM37B A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract:
This talk highlights mismatches between biodiversity data standards and practical ecological and conservation work in freshwater ecosystems, with a botanical focus. Drawing on NIVA’s experience, we demonstrate why ecologists still need taxonomic groupings such as agg., col., vel., /, sensu lato, and sensu stricto. The talk gives aims to show that honest and effective biodiversity reporting requires standards that allow uncertainty to be expressed-rather than erased.

We will present graphs illustrating how substantial amounts of monitoring data can effectively be cut out from time series, ascf. and grouping annotations are not supported in GBIF. At the same time, we emphasize that management categories should be applied as downstream filters, not embedded in global biodiversity infrastructures.

Further, as hybrids and unresolved taxa are common across many organism groups. Mappers are indirectly pushed towards making uncertain species records that are not flagged for uncertainties, due to requirements linked to red listing, Water Framework Directive monitoring, and invasive species mapping. Combined with a lack of verifiability, this creates serious challenges for biologists-both in carrying out their commissioned work and in submitting truthful, high-quality data to GBIF.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Bernard Glauskedalen' (ASR). Co-presented with NIVA database colleague Natalie (surname not given), who the moderator noted was missing from the original slide. The title was announced as changed ('...Need Grouping and Uncertainties'). An extended audience discussion of the posed question is included.

content_items.summary: Bernhard Askedalen and colleague Natalie performed a sketch in which a botanist tries to record uncertain water plant identifications (cf., agg., col., sensu lato) and a database cannot store them, so records are either overstated or bumped to genus, losing ecological information. They showed herbarium sheets with multiple conflicting determinations and noted that for some groups initial names can be as low as 6% correct on expert revision. Natalie found cf. in only 0.1% of water plant and 1.1% of benthic algae observations in NIVA datasets, because reporting pipelines drop uncertainty. They asked how systems should represent uncertainty and taxonomic groupings consistently; the audience suggested keeping these qualifiers with the data, flexibility across organism groups, an identification-uncertainty term, and a BIMS-style identification certainty column with include/exclude decisions.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Biodiversity data systems must be able to record identification uncertainty and taxonomic groupings, or ecologists face a choice between false certainty and lost ecological information.
content_items.why_it_matters: Monitoring data used for ecological status assessments routinely contain cf., aggregates and sensu lato concepts; standards that erase them degrade both data honesty and usability.
key_points: Sketch: 'cf.' for a sterile Sparganium angustifolium cannot be recorded, so it is entered as certain; Utricularia vulgaris without flowers is bumped to genus by a red-list data check; 'agg.', 'col.' and 'sensu lato' are not supported.
Genus-level records lose information useful for within-lake trends and ecological condition assessment based on species assemblages (e.g. eutrophication tolerance).
Paying customers provide little incentive to make records verifiable.

Herbarium sheets can carry three to six different names from different people; for some groups the first name given can be as low as 6% correct, with 94% separated as another species on expert revision.
In selected NIVA datasets from the 1960s to last year, cf. appeared in only 0.1% of water plant and 1.1% of benthic algae observations.
Information exists internally but is lost or transformed when reporting to national systems: uncertain identifications reported as certain, reduced to genus, or aggregates handled via pseudo-taxa.
Question posed: how should biodiversity systems represent uncertainty and taxonomic grouping consistently without losing ecological meaning?

programme.title: How does human impact change species diversity and composition in 50 types of inland water habitats?
programme.session: SYM37B A consensus taxonomic reference for improved freshwater biodiversity data and knowledge
programme.abstract: The revision of inland water habitats for the European Nature Information System (EUNIS) is based on the common types used for the EU Water Framework Directive and related habitat types of the Habitats Directive, as well as on more specific habitats of the Habitats Directive. The presentation describes natural biodiversity for major biological groups in 50 inland water habitat types and how these groups change with human impact. Altogether 23 standing water habitat types and 27 running water habitat types are presented in terms of their natural abiotic conditions and their truly aquatic biological communities, including species richness and characteristic, common and dominant taxa of phytoplankton, aquatic vegetation and fish in standing waters, as well as benthic algae, aquatic vegetation, benthic invertebrates and fish in running waters. The data are based on harmonised taxa lists for each major taxonomic group. While habitats in reference condition have distinct biological communities shaped mainly by geology, altitude, and size, impacted habitats converge towards degraded states with fewer characteristic species due to major pressures, such as nutrient pollution, hydromorphological change and water abstraction. With the EU Biodiversity Strategy 2030 and Nature Restoration Regulation, Europe now has a shared scientific framework to support the monitoring of whether restoration actions effectively improve inland water ecosystems. The work is published as a report from the European Topic Centre for Biodiversity and Ecosystems funded by the European Environment Agency (EEA).

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Anne Luke Solheim'; she introduced herself earlier as 'Anne Lykke Solheim' from NIVA (ASR). ASR renders EUNIS as 'UNIS'.

content_items.summary: Anne Lyche Solheim presented work for the European Environment Agency (European Topic Centre on Biodiversity and Ecosystems) revising EUNIS inland water habitat types to align with Water Framework Directive and Habitats Directive types: over 20 standing and over 20 running water types, described mainly by altitude, calcium/alkalinity, humic content and size. Using REBECCA and WISER project data (2004-2011) with expert-harmonised taxonomy, the team compared natural and impacted water bodies by NMDS and clustering and identified characteristic, common and dominant taxa. Natural waters showed distinct, textbook communities, while human impact made habitat types more similar, with fewer characteristic species (e.g. loss of chrysophytes and isoetids, more cyprinids and fewer salmonids).
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Human pressures erase the natural distinctness of freshwater habitat types, making their biological communities converge on degraded states with fewer characteristic species.
content_items.why_it_matters: The revised EUNIS types and their biological descriptions underpin European habitat reporting and show biotic homogenisation as a measurable outcome of pressure, relevant to stalled Water Framework Directive progress.
key_points: EUNIS is the EEA's European Nature Information System for habitat classification; its freshwater part mixed very broad and very narrow types and needed revision.
Revised types: over 20 standing and over 20 running water habitat types based on WFD broad types, plus rarer Habitats Directive types.
Key type descriptors for biology are much the same for lakes and rivers: altitude, calcium (alkalinity), humic content and size.

Data came from EU projects REBECCA and WISER (2004-2011) covering thousands of lakes and rivers with physicochemical data; taxonomy was harmonised in expert workshops and checked against AlgaeBase and freshwaterecology.info.
Methods: split natural vs impacted water bodies, assess compositional similarity with NMDS and clustering, identify characteristic, common and dominant taxa per habitat.

Natural lakes: richness increases with size and decreases with altitude; e.g. mixotrophic chrysophytes in siliceous, high-altitude and humic lakes; isoetids in siliceous lakes; salmonids in siliceous, high-altitude lakes.

Impacted lakes: types become more similar, fewer characteristic taxa, fewer chrysophytes, fewer isoetids, no characteristic fish species, more cyprinids and fewer salmonids; species richness differences were unclear.
Rivers face multiple pressures; impacts increase similarity between types and reduce characteristic vegetation and invertebrate taxa, with more dominant fish species.
WFD ecological status has stalled at about 60% less than good and 40% good or better since the first river basin management plans in 2009.

entities.name: European Topic Centre on Biodiversity and Ecosystems

datasets: REBECCA and WISER lake and river biological datasets
methods: reference vs impacted comparison using WFD status

notable_claims.claim: Human impact increases the similarity of biological communities between habitat types, which become less specific for all three lake groups.
Impacted lakes of any type had no characteristic fish species, with more cyprinids and fewer salmonids.
Since the first river basin management plans in 2009, WFD ecological status has stood still at about 60% less than good and 40% good or better.

results_findings: Each revised habitat type differs from others for at least one biological community.
Healthy waters have distinct communities shaped by geology, altitude and size.
Impacted habitats converge toward degraded states with fewer characteristic species.
limitations: No clear species richness difference between natural and impacted lakes, possibly due to taxonomic uncertainty in the database.
future_work: EEA will publish a crosswalk table between the old and new classifications and related typologies.
examples_case_studies: Revised EUNIS inland water habitat types (about 50 types)

q_and_a.question: The moderator asked how reference/pristine and impacted sites were defined.
q_and_a.answer_summary: Using WFD ecological status classes already in the database (high/good vs moderate/poor/bad), with GIS help from a topic centre partner to identify reference rivers and officially reported WFD status where missing.

q_and_a.question: An audience member asked whether the old and new classifications can be translated.
q_and_a.answer_summary: A large Excel crosswalk to the old EUNIS system, Habitats Directive types, WFD broad types, IUCN and MAES classifications will be published by the EEA.

representative_excerpt.text: Human impact make many habitats lose their natural distinctness. Different freshwater habitat types become biologically more similar, converging towards degraded states with fewer characteristic species.
